summary: Discusses requirements for inter-AS MPLS Traffic Engineering, presenting scenarios and general guidelines for solutions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a delivery route crosses several companies' roads, they must cooperate. This memo lists what is needed for that kind of route planning.

questions: what is inter-as mpls traffic engineering
why is bgp not enough for traffic engineering
subtitle: Why providers want MPLS traffic-engineered paths that cross autonomous system borders, and what a solution must do.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering could be used only inside one autonomous system, yet providers want bandwidth guarantees, resource optimization and fast recovery for paths that cross AS boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five application scenarios and then lists detailed requirements for a solution: signaling and path computation, optimality, diverse paths, re-optimization, fast reroute, DS-TE support, scalability, management, and for multi-provider cases confidentiality and policy control.
tldr.outcome: It sets guidelines for solutions and makes no claim that a practical solution can meet every requirement. It is informational.

facts.label: Core objectives
facts.value: Bandwidth guarantees, resource optimization, fast recovery

today: RFC 4216 is an Informational document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements and scenarios only; it specifies no protocol and makes no claim that a solution can meet every requirement.

sections.title: The Problem at AS Borders
sections.content:
The MPLS traffic engineering (TE) mechanism of RFC 3209 can help service providers (SPs) meet three goals: supporting end-to-end services that need QoS guarantees, optimizing network resources, and providing fast recovery. However, it can only be used within an autonomous system (AS). This document sets out requirements for an inter-AS mechanism that achieves the same goals across AS boundaries, within or beyond one SP's administrative domain.

Other kinds of traffic engineering exist: IGP metric-based within an AS and BGP attribute-based across ASes. They give coarser control of traffic paths. This RFC addresses only a fine-grained, MPLS-based approach, and only IP/MPLS networks, because there is not enough interest in inter-AS TE for IP-only networks at this time. It also says it makes no claim that a practical solution meeting all its requirements is possible.
sections.eli5: Planning a trip inside one town is easy. Planning one that crosses many towns, each with its own rules, is harder, and this document explains why people want it.

sections.title: Three Objectives
sections.content:
Bandwidth guarantees. Diffserv mechanisms can enforce QoS policies, but where strict bounds are needed, admission control inside the backbone is sometimes required too. The typical example is VoIP traffic in the EF class, which needs bandwidth guaranteed along an end-to-end path. When that path crosses several ASes, the guarantee has to cross them too.

Resource optimization. BGP is used between ASes and can also steer traffic, but its facilities are coarse. As the number of inter-AS links grows, or when links join different SPs, uncoordinated routing changes make inter-AS policies complex and hard to scale. A more granular mechanism is then needed alongside BGP.

Fast recovery. Customers expect VoIP and similar services to keep the same packet loss and availability across ASes as inside one. That calls for stable, fast convergence on link, SRLG or node failures, which the RFC calls difficult with current inter-domain techniques, especially for failures between ASBRs or of an ASBR node. The RFC extends the existing intra-AS MPLS TE across inter-AS links because implementations and operational experience already exist.
sections.eli5: Three wishes: a guaranteed lane, a smart way to use the roads, and a quick detour if a bridge breaks.

sections.title: How BGP Does TE Today
sections.content:
Appendix A summarizes the current BGP-based practices. One is "closest exit" routing, where egress traffic follows the lowest IGP or intra-AS MPLS TE metric to the BGP next hop. The other chooses egress paths with BGP path attributes such as AS_PATH, MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) and Local_Pref, according to peering or transit policies. Routes can also be tagged with an attribute when announced to another AS, steering ingress traffic toward certain PoPs or regions.

SPs have faced non-deterministic factors in these practices: sub-optimum traffic distribution across inter-AS links, and traffic changes caused by uncoordinated IGP or BGP policy changes in other ASes, such as MED or AS-prepend.
sections.eli5: Today providers steer traffic by telling neighbors which door is preferred. It works, but when a neighbor changes its mind, the traffic jumps around.

sections.title: Five Application Scenarios
sections.content:
Scenario I, extended or virtual PoP. A global SP1 expands into a region where a regional SP2 is denser, co-locating aggregation routers in SP2's PoPs. Inter-AS MPLS TE LSPs between SP1's ASBR or PE and those routers secure the capacity SP2 provides.

Scenario II, extended or virtual trunk. SP1 aggregates customer VPN sites onto an SP2 PE router, and a TE tunnel runs from there to SP1's network. Case 1 treats the tunnel as a virtual trunk, case 2 as a virtual local access link.

Scenario III, end-to-end from CE to CE. Customers want a TE tunnel from CE1 to CE2 across several SPs. The RFC says this will not scale well in a partial or full mesh, so few deployments are expected unless hierarchical intra-AS LSPs reduce signaling state.

Scenario IV, multiple ASes in one SP. An SP with ASes across continents or regions, where inter-region capacity is expensive, can optimize resources with inter-AS TE LSPs, and an inter-AS DS-TE LSP could carry L2 pseudo wires or VoIP with bandwidth needs.

Scenario V, transit ASes. SP1 links a regional network to its backbone through transit ASes of SP2, SP3 and others, or uses such a tunnel as backup for an internal path, which could add routing complexity.
sections.eli5: Each scenario is a different story of one company borrowing other companies' roads and wanting a promise that its trucks get through.

sections.title: Requirements Within One Provider
sections.content:
The solution MUST interoperate seamlessly with current intra-AS MPLS TE and inherit its capabilities from RFC 3209. It SHOULD allow a TE LSP to be provisioned at the head-end with end-to-end RSVP signaling, possibly with loose paths, across the ASBRs with no extra provisioning along the way. It SHOULD let operators pick or auto-discover AS numbers as loose hops and LSRs including ASBRs, record them in the Explicit Route Object and Record Route Object, and exclude nodes or resources.

It SHOULD allow an optimal path, defined as minimal end-to-end cost by IGP or TE metric, while allowing sub-optimality because a path may not stay optimal. Across ASes with different IGP metric policies, IGP metric normalization might be needed. It SHOULD set up link, SRLG or node diverse LSPs. It MUST re-optimize non-disruptively, on a timer, a network event or a manual request, give the head-end control over whether to re-optimize, and be able to reject re-optimization at AS boundaries.

Fast recovery SHOULD interoperate with MPLS TE fast reroute, protecting against link failure and node failure inside an AS or at its boundary. The solution SHOULD satisfy the DS-TE requirements. It MUST have minimum impact on scalability for IGP, BGP and RSVP-TE, and SHOULD allow aggregation of tunnels into aggregating LSPs. It SHOULD offer several ways to map traffic onto tunnels, including announcing a tunnel as a link into IS-IS or OSPF. Management needs an inter-AS TE MIB that extends existing MIBs, and fault detection should interoperate with intra-AS mechanisms. The solution MUST allow extensions and SHOULD NOT add unnecessary complexity or impact existing BGP-based TE or MPLS TE, and its performance SHOULD be judged on path optimality, setup time, failure and restoration time, and control and forwarding plane overhead.
sections.eli5: Whatever plan people make has to work with the roads and rules that already exist, stay fast when many trucks use it, be able to switch to a better route without stopping traffic, and not become too complicated.

sections.title: Multiple Providers and Security
sections.content:
When the AS borders are also borders between SPs, all the single-provider requirements apply, plus more. Confidentiality: the solution MIGHT allow hiding the hops used by a TE LSP inside an AS, so that A in AS1 can learn that the best path to B goes through ASBR2 without knowing the hops in AS2. The path cost inside AS2 could optionally be provided through PCC-PCE communication.

Policy control: ingress policy controls at AS boundaries let SPs enforce interconnect agreements or modify requested parameters. Policies could cover RSVP-TE session attributes (affinities and preemption priorities), per-AS or per-SP bandwidth admission control, the request origin, DS-TE TE-Class, fast reroute attributes, and whether optimization is allowed. A policy server MAY be used and implementations SHOULD allow it. A non-compliant request SHOULD trigger an RSVP Path Error toward the head-end, which SHOULD act, for example by rerouting. Attributes may be rewritten at the boundary, again with a Path Error indicating the change. Traffic policing on inter-AS links SHOULD ensure that traffic does not exceed the bandwidth negotiated at LSP signaling.

The Security Considerations section says solutions MUST address security across SP administrative domains. No new security extensions beyond intra-AS TE are expected, but a trusted model across AS boundaries needs more consideration. SPs SHOULD be able to authenticate, for example with the RSVP INTEGRITY Object, allow and possibly deny inter-AS signaling requests, and be protected from DoS attacks.
sections.eli5: When the roads belong to different companies, each one wants to keep its map private, set limits on how much it carries for others, and make sure strangers cannot give fake orders.

viz.caption: THE THREE GOALS OF INTER-AS TRAFFIC ENGINEERING

items.title: Bandwidth guarantees
items.text: Admission control and reserved bandwidth along a path that crosses ASes, for example for EF class VoIP.

items.title: Resource optimization
items.text: Finer control than BGP-based practices as inter-AS links grow in number.

items.title: Fast recovery
items.text: Stable, quick convergence on link, SRLG and ASBR node failures.

viz.caption: THE FIVE SCENARIOS AT A GLANCE

cells: SP1 uses SP2's PoPs as extended transport
Tunnel from SP2's PE to SP1's network
Tunnel end to end across several SPs
Primary or backup tunnel over transit ASes
